newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Surgical closes in on Circon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Surgical closes in on Circon.

text.p: U.S. Surgical Corp is tightening its grip on endoscopy company Circon Corp as chances of a "white knight" bidder stepping in fade.

U.S. Surgical on Friday expressed confidence it would would be able to complete the deal at $18 a share, saying that the shares thus far tendered, combined with those it already owns, represent 63 percent of Circon's outstanding stock.
Analysts did not rule out a white knight snatching Circon from U.S. Surgical. But since the hostile $230 million bid was launched August 2, none has publicly surfaced.
"I would have thought they would have come in by this point had there been an interest," said Robinson-Humphrey analyst John Runningen.
The next phase in the struggle could be a court battle over Circon's recently adopted poison pill, analysts and deal specialists said.
The news that U.S. Surgical has access to 63 percent of its shares "should have (Circon management) shaken up a little," one arbitrager said.
But, he warned, "there's so such thing as a done deal until you have a check in your hand."
Circon's shares were trading at the deal price Friday afternoon, up 5/8 at 18. U.S. Surgical rose 1/4 to 36-1/2.

U.S. Surgical said about seven million Circon shares have been tendered. With the one million Circon shares it already owned, U.S. Surgical needs about 1.7 million more to close the deal, a U.S. Surgical spokesman said.
U.S. Surgical extended the tender offer, which was due to expire Thursday, through September 30.
"We're very pleased with the shareholders' response," the spokesman for Norwalk Conn.-based U.S. Surgical said. "They've clearly demonstrated that they support our offer at $18."

Earlier this month, Santa Barbara-based Circon's board rejected the offer and adopted a poison pill takeover defense, saying the U.S. Surgical deal "did not reflect the long-term values inherent in the company."
If the fight ends up in court, the battle between the two companies could drag on for several months, said Piper Jaffray analyst Thomas Gunderson.
Potential rival suitors named by analysts include Johnson and Johnson, Stryker Corp, London-based Smith & Nephew Plc and Germany's B. Braun Melsungen AG.
Spokesmen at J&J and Smith & Nephew declined comment on Circon, while Braun and Stryker were not immediately available.
"If another contender for Circon doesn't show up in 30 days it makes it very difficult for Circon not to talk to U.S. Surgical," Gunderson said.
Circon had no immediate comment but a spokeswoman said the company may respond to U.S. Surgical's latest statement on Friday.
Circon makes endoscopes, which are miniature camaras that allow surgeons to view internal organs, make diagnoses and monitor minimally invasive surgery.
Acquiring Circon will allow U.S. Surgical to expand its $500 million minimially invasive product lines and offer surgeons a package of endoscopes and surgical instruments, analysts said.

Other potential bidders "are pursing other avenues to grow their business," Runningen said. "For U.S. Surgical it is a natural fit, so I don't expect a white knight to come riding in and bid the price up."
--New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1733
